title: Should Your First Consequence Be A Warning? https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/05/15/should-your-first-consequence-be-a-warning/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin answers a frequently asked question—whether a warning should be the first consequence for misbehavior—with an emphatic yes, arguing it eliminates three common, stress-inducing habits: reminding students of rules, glaring at them, and verbally correcting them on the spot. He illustrates each ineffective habit with a short classroom vignette showing how reminding, glaring, and correcting leave teachers stressed and students still misbehaving. By contrast, a simple, consistently applied warning is easy to enforce consistently, avoids personal confrontation, builds student trust through predictability, requires no interruption to teaching, is stress-free for the teacher, and gives students a clear sense of what to expect. He notes that a warning only works when it is backed by a genuinely unwelcome second consequence, previewing a follow-up article on delivering warnings effectively.
points: A warning as the first consequence eliminates three common, stress-inducing habits: reminding, glaring, and correcting students.
Reminding, glaring, and correcting all leave teachers stressed and frustrated while failing to reliably change behavior.
A simple warning is easy to apply consistently, avoids personal confrontation, and builds student trust through predictability.
Warnings require no interruption to teaching and are stress-free compared to persuasion, intimidation, or repeated correction.
A warning only functions effectively when it's backed by a strong, genuinely unwelcome second consequence.
quotes: I’m frequently asked whether I recommend giving a warning as a first consequence. My answer is an emphatic yes.
Mrs. Fowler often reminds her students to follow classroom rules. Predictably, they break them often.
Mr. Penn is proud of his ability to stop misbehavior in its tracks with his well-practiced “look” but has grown tired of the constant battles to get students to follow his rules.
When you have a classroom management plan that includes a warning, it takes the guesswork out of handling initial misbehavior. Student breaks rule…teacher gives warning.
Doing exactly what you say you will do builds your students’ trust in you, which makes it easier to influence behavior.
You don’t have to rely on persuasion or intimidation to stop misbehavior. You don’t have to yell, remind, glare, or use any of the other stress inducing methods.
